articles.title_orig: China’s Military Purges Accelerate
articles.title_zh: China’s Military Purges Accelerate
articles.content_orig:
When China’s leader, Xi Jinping, endorsed the expulsion of dozens of disgraced officials at a recent Communist Party meeting in Beijing, one man stood out as a clear winner.
Taking his new place at the front of the meeting was Gen. Zhang Shengmin, the somber-faced enforcer of Mr. Xi’s purges inside the military. He had been promoted to the Politburo, the party’s top leadership council, the latest step in his improbable rise from low-profile inspector to a position second only to Mr. Xi in China’s military hierarchy.
General Zhang has been the principal overseer of Mr. Xi’s campaign to purify the People’s Liberation Army. His latest elevation signaled that the investigations, indoctrination drives and loyalty tests could continue for years, as Mr. Xi searches for officers he believes are irreproachably loyal, experts and officials said.
“Twist the blade inward, with strict measures to cure disorder,” China’s main military newspaper said after the party meeting that was held late last month, referring to the continued discipline campaign.
Three officials in Taiwan said they believed Mr. Xi’s loyalty campaign would keep the Chinese military focused on its own problems. That could hinder preparations for possible war over Taiwan, the self-governed island democracy that Beijing claims. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal assessments.
The leadership uncertainty comes as China’s military has continued to pressure Taiwan. Dozens of P.L.A. ships held unannounced drills in seas off the Chinese coast in recent weeks, with some, including a carrier strike group, still remaining, Joseph Wu , the secretary-general of Taiwan’s National Security Council, posted on X on Thursday.

articles.title_orig: In China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism
articles.title_zh: In China, Nvidia scandal stirs defiance and skepticism
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.
Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.
Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."
Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.
There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.
Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.
Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq falls on Friday as Nvidia keeps sliding, but major averages are up for week: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq falls on Friday as Nvidia keeps sliding, but major averages are up for week: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build.
But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation f rom Nvidia at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that's powering the artificial intelligence boom.
In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China , made the company he co-founded the world's most valuable.
Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was "indispensable" but "the graveyards are filled with indispensable men," referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle.
While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang's charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate.
"I'm not sure we've seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world's largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal," Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC.
Whoever follows will "face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder," he added.
Apple 's image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor.
Tim Cook invested in Apple's chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple's supply chain.
Cook had "considerable preparation" for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple's market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure.
Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet in 2019, 21 years after founding Google.
Page and Brin's departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the "natural time" to simplify the company's management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai.
Travis Kalanick left Uber in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns.
But his departure "unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing," Withers added.
Former Expedia CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability .
Withers said successor CEOs often struggle "under normal circumstances" to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership.
"It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company's founder," he added.
Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies.
Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company.
"We're talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That's a pretty remarkable situation," he added.
As well as having to "step out of his shadow," the new CEO will have to deal with the "scandal" arising from Huang's conduct and "the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia," Withers said.
Huang's successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy,  while picking up the relationships he managed.
Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May . Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world's second-largest economy.
He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company's key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung.
Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain.
The supply chain was "where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology," Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially "when supply chains are already so tight."
Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.
Investors noted that the new CEO will have a roadmap of products for the next few years, unaffected by Huang's removal.
"We have to look beyond Jensen ... there are thousands upon thousands of engineers," Joanne Feeney, partner and portfolio manager, Advisors Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday, as pressure was mounting on Huang to go.

articles.title_orig: Before he was Pope Leo, he was their bishop. Now he’s back home.
articles.title_zh: Before he was Pope Leo, he was their bishop. Now he’s back home.
articles.content_orig:
LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV made a triumphant return Friday to the Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for eight years and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto.”
Leo arrived in a plane decorated with “#LeoXFliesHome” stickers and he was greeted with a sign at the airport bearing the same message. A small dance troupe performed before him as he stepped off the plane.
He will stay in the area until Sunday to lead eight events, including a private dinner with the priests who once reported to him as bishop.
The crowds greeting Leo in Peru’s fourth largest city will likely be smaller than the estimated 3 million or so who welcomed the pope when he arrived Wednesday in Lima, the country’s capital.
But their enthusiasm more than made up for their smaller numbers as the former Bishop Robert Prevost of Chiclayo returned to this coastal city of nearly 700,000 as the leader of the  Catholic Church.
As toured in an open-air popemobile at the Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert plain just outside Chiclayo, the crowd erupted in cheers, many waving waved white-and-yellow Vatican flags.
Some had been waiting since last night to catch a glimpse of the pontiff, many of them forced to walk as lines of cars had blocked the roads where vendors sold hats, mini pope dolls and sweet Peruvian bread.
Maria Esther Chozo Reyes, 76, said she had taken a 12-hour bus ride from Lima and arrived Thursday afternoon before she camped overnight. “He knows the people of Chiclayo and he’s lived here, he’s made his mission here,” she told The Associated Press. “We really need his blessing.”
Thanking the people for their love and support, in his sermon Leo said it was a blessing to be in his former home.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer ⁠of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said, adding that his lung cancer disgnosis and surgery to remove part of one lung exactly a month ago had been a time of trial.
Leo’s sojourn to Chiclayo is midway through the final leg of his 12-day visit to South America , a historic trip that included stops in Argentina and Uruguay. And it’s the most sentimental part of his journey.
For while Leo was born in Chicago and English is his mother tongue, the first words he uttered from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica was a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved Diocese of Chiclayo.”
During his time in that city, Leo often repeated a joke: “Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter.”
Setting aside the fact that it’s actually two letters, Leo quickly became a beloved figure in Chiclayo by championing social justice issues, embracing the poor and venturing into the local prison to say Mass.
During the pandemic, Leo endeared himself to many by launching a fundraising drive to raise money for a badly-needed oxygen production plant.
When Cyclone Maku hit the area in March 2023, Leo was photographed wading through the floodwaters to get supplies to the destitute and distributing food at soup kitchens.
At Christmastime, Leo would drive a pickup truck laden with gifts into remote villages around Chiclayo and join family celebrations.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary, priest and finally as a bishop in Peru and became a citizen in 2015. During his two decades in the country, he was also a strident critic of then- Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori’s authoritarian regime .
On Thursday, Leo delivered a speech while sitting beside Fujimori’s daughter, recently-elected Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional performing arts center.
Leo urged the country’s leaders to cultivate honesty and integrity to strengthen public trust --- and called on officeholders to listen to their constituents.
“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said.
There was thunderous applause when Leo referred to Peru as “my homeland.”
And Leo appeared to have tears in his eyes as he sang the Peruvian national anthem along with a children’s choir.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Lima and Corky Siemaszko from New York.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Europe pushes for a seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks a unified voice
articles.title_zh: Europe pushes for a seat at Ukraine peace talks‌ but lacks a unified voice
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. Now they finally expect to get one, and they don’t know who should sit in it.
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said on Thursday.
Mr. Kushner’s dig reflected a harsh — and, for Europe, potentially embarrassing — reality that internal divisions could cost European officials time and influence. Mr. Kushner and his fellow U.S. negotiator, Steve Witkoff, pushed this week to add Europe to the talks after Russia insisted during discussions in the United Arab Emirates that postwar security in Europe be a topic of negotiation.
Russian negotiators made it clear during the talks with Ukraine and the United States that as a condition of ending the war, they want Europe to change how it protects itself. Russia has a record of pushing to pare back NATO operations near its border.
European officials have rejected those suggestions, insisting that the continent, not the Kremlin, decides its security.

articles.title_orig: China’s top diplomat calls for expanding cooperation in meeting with South Korean minister
articles.title_zh: China’s top diplomat calls for expanding cooperation in meeting with South Korean minister
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING, Nov 13 (Reuters) – China is willing to expand cooperation with South Korea in traditional and emerging sectors including ​artificial intelligence and biomedicine, Foreign Minister ‌Wang Yi said on Friday.
• In a meeting with his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun, Wang said the two countries are “close neighbours that cannot be ‌moved ​away” and “maintaining good-neighbourliness and ⁠friendship is the right ⁠choice for both sides,” according to a statement released by China’s Foreign Ministry
• The South Korean diplomat is on a ​two-day visit to China starting Friday
• China-South Korea relations were “back onto the right ⁠track” after their leaders’ ⁠exchanges since late last year, Wang ​said
• Ties soured under Yoon Suk Yeol, the ​predecessor of South Korean President Lee ‌Jae Myung, who drew Seoul closer to Washington and Tokyo
• Lee, who took office in June 2025, has sought to restore ⁠relations, hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Gyeongju in late 2025 and making a state visit to ⁠China in ‌January
• China is willing to ⁠further enhance mutual trust with ​South ‌Korea and expand their common interests, ​Wang said
• ⁠Next week, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will visit China and attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen
(Reporting by Shi Bu and Ryan Woo; Editing by ​Xevi Fontdegloria)

articles.title_orig: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Rosenberg: Uncompromising Putin ups demands for peace with Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin says he wishes "eternal peace" for Ukraine.
That is the same Russian president who ordered the full-scale invasion of Russia's neighbour nearly five years ago and who continues to reject the idea of a comprehensive ceasefire.
And what, in Moscow's view, is a prerequisite for peace?
The Kremlin spelt it out after talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner: "A new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace."
Translated from Kremlin-speak, it means Moscow wants to change the security set-up of Europe in a way that benefits Russia.
What Russia is pushing for is, potentially, the biggest change to European security arrangements since the end of the Cold War.
The Kremlin has put back on the table its controversial proposal from December 2021 – the "draft treaties" with the US and Nato which would not only have put the brakes on the alliance's eastward enlargement by giving Moscow cast-iron guarantees that, for instance, Ukraine and Georgia would never be allowed to join, but also rolled back Nato military infrastructure from countries of central and eastern Europe which became Nato members following the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Western leaders dismissed such demands as an unacceptable Russian ultimatum. Two months later Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The "draft treaties" were put away. Now they are out of the geopolitical filing cabinet, and being quoted again by the Kremlin.
What is more, Yuri Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy aide, has suggested that Moscow is about to "add certain new considerations" to its list of demands in light of Western efforts "to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia".
That does not mean, of course, that Western governments will accept them.
But the fact that the question of European security is featuring now in discussions on Ukraine is viewed here as a victory for Moscow.
"In December 2021 Russia actively proposed that Nato rethink the security system in Europe," wrote newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda earlier this week.
"Our proposals were almost laughed at.
"Having secured one victory by forcing the West to think about security, our diplomats need a second by making the West heed Russia's concerns about Nato enlargement."
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, has called Russia's demands for a new European security architecture a "trap" designed to "shift attention away from a ceasefire".
"The sequencing of Ukraine-Russia talks is important," Kallas wrote on social media. "The priority should be securing a ceasefire, followed by a peace agreement. Only then can there be discussions on Europe's wider security architecture."
Europe's problem is that, right now, it is not at the table.
Moscow has had no desire to give it a chair. It has slammed European leaders for their military support for Kyiv and tough stance on Russia.
This week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi involved Ukraine, Russia and the US.
After his discussions in Moscow, Witkoff indicated that Putin had agreed to the idea of European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks.
But on Friday the Kremlin indicated a final decision on European participation had not been taken.
"Once we understand their true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to take a decision about dialogue on Ukraine in a wider format," said Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov.
At the talks with Witkoff and Kushner he was sounding uncompromising and confident.
The Americans are knocking at his door and seeking a deal and the Europeans are contemplating contacts with him. Last month the leaders of Norway and Finland reached out and called him.
And next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, Putin may have a separate meeting with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. Russian media are already comparing them to the "Big Three" - Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill - who met in 1945 to reorganise post-World War Two Europe.
And yet, after nearly five years of war, Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield.
The Russian economy is under increasing pressure.
Ukrainian drone strikes continue to target Russian oil refineries, sparking fears of new fuel shortages.
But, so far, none of this has convinced the Kremlin leader to end the fighting.

articles.title_orig: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.title_zh: Investors Warn Bond Rout Isn’t Over After Week of Soaring Yields
articles.content_orig:
The 10-year Treasury yield stayed over 5% on Friday after October's producer price index , a measure of wholesale prices, came in slightly less than expected.
The yield — the key benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose 3 basis points to 5.133%. It reached a high of 5.174% earlier in the day.
The 2-year Treasury note yield, typically more sensitive to short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was lower by less than 1 basis point at 4.855%. The longer-dated 30-year Treasury bond yield, sensitive to geopolitical risks, was 4 basis points higher at 5.47%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
October's producer price index rose 0.3% versus September, less than the 0.4% expected by economists polled by Dow Jones. But on an annual basis, PPI rose 6.5% over the past 12 months, the biggest annual increase since November 2022.
There was "no silver lining" in the inflation report, said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS, adding that core PPI — which excludes  food, energy and trade services — increased 0.5% in October.
"It is economics 101 that producer prices lead consumer prices and right now it looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of factory inflation," he said.
The moves come after 10-year Treasury yields jumped more than 13 basis points to more than 5% in Thursday's session , with the 2-year yield soaring more than 15 basis points.
Investors now see a Federal Reserve rate hike next month as a certainty. Traders are pricing in 100% odds of a rise at the Dec. 9 meeting, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Odds of a quarter percentage point hike now stand at 86%, with the chance of a half point increase at around 14%.
Energy inflation remains a key part of the puzzle, with oil set for its second weekly decline as prospects of renewed strikes by the U.S. against Iran fade. Prices were choppy in early trading Friday. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for December delivery were down 0.1% at $88.63 per barrel. Brent crude , the international oil benchmark, was higher by 0.3% at $96.11.

articles.title_orig: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.title_zh: Windows 0-day dropped by disgruntled researcher hands hackers System rights
articles.content_orig:
Nightmare Eclipse, the pseudonym of a researcher with an ongoing, very public beef with Microsoft, has dropped yet another Windows zero-day.
On Tuesday, Nightmare Eclipse disclosed SignDrop, a vulnerability that gives local users full System rights on some versions of Windows. The vulnerability resides in the Common Log File System , which Microsoft describes as a “general-purpose logging service used by software clients running in user-mode or kernel-mode.” By forcing a privileged process such as Windows Defender to open a crafted CLFS container, an attacker with ordinary user rights can abuse the privileged file creation to elevate privileges to System.
The attack exploits the interaction of CLFS, Windows Defender, and Windows file permissions. The exploit uses Windows Defender to open a log file created by a standard user by calling ServerMpUpdateEngineSignature, a legitimate Defender function for processing antivirus signature updates.
By manipulating Windows Object Manager symbolic links, the attacker causes Defender to open the CLFS container in the security context of the antimalware engine. If an associated authentication file is missing, CLFS creates it using Defender’s System privileges. Because CLFS assigns the newly created file the Discretionary Access Control List of the original file, the attacker may gain access to a file created with System privileges, allowing the file-creation operation to be abused as part of a privilege-escalation attack.
Ironically, the vulnerability stems from a security measure Microsoft introduced in October 2025 to prevent attackers from exploiting other vulnerabilities in CLFS.
“If everything is chained correctly, funnily this legit security mitigation can be used against itself and allow an elevation [of] privileges,” Nightmare Eclipse wrote . “Everything is done properly by Microsoft here but the logic allows abuse.”
What makes it funnier is the fact that it can be used against any antimalware engine to bypass their self defense (or tamper protection) mechanism as you can trigger arbitrary file creation in the context of their own antimalware process so from the perspective of their kernel drivers, the file creation request is coming from their own legit process so it passes, this makes this vulnerability unique as it can be used to turn off any antivirus/EDR.
Nightmare Eclipse said the exploit worked against Windows 11 26H2, Windows 11 26H2 Experimental, and Windows Server 2025 Experimental. People can see if their systems are vulnerable by checking the CLFS authentication mode. If it’s in learning mode or enforcement mode, the system is vulnerable, and the PoC supplied in the post should spawn a SYSTEM shell. Nightmare Eclipse has published numerous other Windows zero-days in recent months.
Researcher Will Dormann said in an interview that he has been able to reproduce the exploit and that it works as described, but not on all versions of Windows 11. But there’s a catch, he said.
“The requirements are important in that it seems to require Windows 26H2, and one that has existed for more than 90 days, it seems,” he explained. “That is, you can’t just take a new 26H2 system and install updates and have it work.”
For a system to be vulnerable, Dormann said, the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\CLFS\Authentication\Mode value must be 0 or 1.” Of the many machines Dormann uses, only a single one met this requirement.
Microsoft does staged rollouts of Windows updates, such as 26H2, so it’s not clear how many people have it. You can check by running the “winver” command. Microsoft representatives didn’t respond to an email seeking comment.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX to attempt first Starship spacecraft recovery on land in 15th flight
articles.title_zh: SpaceX to attempt first Starship spacecraft recovery on land in 15th flight
articles.content_orig:
A crucial test today could bring SpaceX one step closer to revolutionizing spaceflight — or cast new uncertainty on the company’s boldest ambitions.
SpaceX will for the first time attempt to bring every part of its massive Starship, the most powerful rocket ever built, back to dry land — intact — during a mission set to launch on Friday between 5:45 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. ET.
The aim is to develop a fully reusable launch system, a goal the company has deemed the “holy grail” of rocketry because it would eliminate the need to throw away multimillion-dollar rocket parts after a single mission. That in turn could dramatically lower the cost of a single launch — by orders of magnitude, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk hopes — and open a new world of possibilities for space exploration.
‘The most complicated launch campaign ever’: NASA lays out mad dash to test lunar landers
But to realize its vision, SpaceX needs to figure out how to bring Starship’s upper half, a 171-foot-tall spacecraft, back from orbit to a safe, upright landing within the arms of the company’s South Texas launch tower.
Such a move has never been demonstrated.
But SpaceX has long made clear that recapturing and reflying the entire Starship vehicle is imperative to achieve some of the company’s most audacious goals and, as the company said in a statement, “unlock the true capability of Starship.”
For decades, space travel has meant throwing away millions of dollars on one-time-use rockets and parts. Enter Starship. If Elon Musk’s SpaceX can “catch” its latest spaceship after it reenters Earth’s atmosphere, the company could change space exploration forever.
The company intends for the gargantuan rocket to tackle a wide range of lofty, extraterrestrial projects — such as helping NASA to establish a permanent human presence on the moon, expand its space-based Starlink internet network, launch an orbital data center, and “extend the light of consciousness to the stars, and make life multiplanetary,” the company said in a statement , nodding to Musk’s longtime goal of using Starship to colonize Mars.
Musk clips his Mars settlement ambition, aims for the moon instead
If all goes according to plan during Friday’s test, SpaceX will put on an extraordinary show beginning just minutes after liftoff. That’s when the bottom half of the Starship, called the Super Heavy rocket booster, is expected to break away from the upper spacecraft — or “ship.”
The booster would then aim to make its own pinpoint landing back at the launch tower. SpaceX has previously demonstrated this maneuver on a few Starship prior test flights, but never with the current version of the vehicle, called V3, which debuted in May.
The company has already pioneered the science of reusing first-stage rocket boosters with its Falcon rockets, saving the company untold millions of dollars.
But attempting to recapture and refly the upper stage of a rocket — as SpaceX will attempt to do in this upcoming test of the upper Starship spacecraft — introduces a host of new risks and challenges, as well as potential rewards.
How two billionaires are shaping America’s return to the moon
After separating from the Super Heavy booster, the ship will ignite its own engines and attempt to reach Earth orbit — a step that SpaceX only narrowly achieved for the first time in September during its last test flight. It requires the spacecraft to relight its engines and reach velocities topping 17,000 miles per hour, or 20 times the speed of sound.
This step alone has numerous risks. Any time SpaceX sends a Starship spacecraft to orbit, mission teams must take extreme care to ensure the vehicle can also make a controlled return to Earth. Otherwise, the ship could make an unpredictable descent back home, threatening people or property.
“Starship is obviously meant to be a reusable launch vehicle and is meant to survive atmospheric reentry,” said Jeremy Pedro, SpaceX’s director of Starship propulsion systems, in a video recently released by SpaceX. “And so it’s really important that we do not leave the vehicle on orbit in the event that it randomly reenters and comes back over landmasses or populated areas.”
If the Starship spacecraft reaches orbit and the flight moves forward, it would complete about 14 laps around the planet over the course of 22 hours. During that time, the vehicle would deploy 26 of SpaceX’s Starlink V3 satellites, which are designed to boost the capacity of the company’s internet service network.
As Starship cruises through orbit, mission controllers will also have several opportunities to bring Starship back to Earth early if something is amiss, sending it to a splashdown in the ocean.
SpaceX’s megarocket is on the verge of paradigm-shifting success. It’s spurring a ‘crisis’
If all goes according to plan, SpaceX would face the nail-biting theatrics of guiding the ship back into the thick inner band of Earth’s atmosphere — a process called reentry — on Saturday afternoon. This stage of the flight creates a violent wave of compression and a buildup of plasma that can drive temperatures outside the spacecraft to more than 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit.
Then, as the vehicle heads for a landing, Starship will have “to come in across the West Coast of the United States, so you’re crossing land, where typically, on most of these missions you’re crossing bodies of water,” said Joseph Gonzalez, an associate professor of practice in aerospace engineering at the University of Illinois. Passing over inhabited areas makes this a particularly high-stakes moment.
SpaceX said on its website that Starship will use four flaps to make “small turns” to intentionally veer over “sparsely populated” areas in its projected path over northern Mexico and southern Texas, reducing the risk of catastrophe if something goes wrong.
Even after reentry, mission controllers can still opt to forgo a landing attempt back at SpaceX’s Starbase facility. Mission controllers will have the option to direct the vehicle to splash down in the Gulf or order the vehicle to self-destruct so that the entire Statue-of-Liberty-size craft doesn’t crash onto land.
But if the mission goes smoothly, in the final moments before the historic touchdown attempt, Starship will pass over the northern part of South Padre Island located off the southern coast of Texas, before turning back toward SpaceX’s Mechazilla launch tower and completing an acrobatic bellyflop maneuver. During its final, parachute-less descent, the ship will use its engines and precision steering to try to guide itself back into the arms of the launch tower.
“The significance behind this, I don’t think people understand,” Gonzalez said. “If this weekend sees very positive results, I’m thinking they can get to a fully reusable rocket in the next two or three years.”
But errors, known in rocketry parlance as “anomalies,” are a very real possibility.
SpaceX has had a series of issues during recent Starship flights with the reliability of the Raptor rocket engines that power Super Heavy and the ship. Some engines have spontaneously ceased firing or failed to relight when they were supposed to.
Those issues were particularly glaring during the last test in September. Called Flight 14, that mission marked the first time SpaceX sought to fly Starship on an orbital trajectory rather than a “passively safe” suborbital one, during which the ship would be more likely to crash into the ocean if it spun out of control.
SpaceX had clarified that it needed to ensure the vehicle was working as intended before giving the ship the green light to head for orbit. But minutes into flight, one of the ship’s engines shut down prematurely and remained out of service for the rest of the flight.
SpaceX Starship splashes down after reaching orbit in unprecedented test flight
Initially, mission controllers — and even the host narrating SpaceX’s livestream — said the company would forgo a second engine burn, opting to avoid the risk of sending the vehicle to orbit.

articles.title_orig: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.title_zh: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.
U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.
The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.
The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”
Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making.
In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy.
“Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states.
That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee.
“The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X.
After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia.
Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress , will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.
Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.
Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.
After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per The Wall Street Journal. Stock fell about 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said . The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.
The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.
According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.
Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed .
The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.
Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported . The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.
Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported . Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.
In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.
On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.
When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia , Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”
Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

Pershing Square Capital CEO Bill Ackman thinks Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) is a great story with a business that has real potential. Just don't expect him to be a buyer early on when Anthropic becomes publicly traded.
"We think of ourselves as very low-risk investors. We want to invest in businesses that we can predict with a very high degree of confidence," the well-known value investor said at Yahoo Finance Invest. "I think Anthropic is perhaps the most amazing business story of this century in terms of from zero to where it is today — it's an absolutely remarkable story. An incredibly impressive story. I think it's just a much more complicated question as to what that business is worth. It's very hard to nail that with any degree of precision. It could be worth a lot more, a lot less, depending upon a few variables that are difficult to predict. And that's why it doesn't fit into our portfolio."
Anthropic has set an IPO price range of $70 to $78 per share, targeting a fully diluted valuation of approximately $1.4 trillion. The company could raise up to $100 billion from its IPO at the high end of the range.
Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
But the business has a lot to prove to justify keeping such a lofty valuation in public markets.
In an amended S-1 filing, Anthropic said that third quarter sales rose 1,127% to $17 billion. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-over-quarter basis. Third quarter sales increased 47% compared with a 144% growth rate in the second quarter. Sales increased 132% in the first quarter.
The company also lost a staggering $23.29 billion in the third quarter.
Anthropic is expected to debut on public markets on Thursday, Nov. 19. It plans to list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.
"I think Anthropic is on the cusp, or might even be at, a place in terms of its operating profitability, where it's real operating profitability," Ackman added. "I think the issue is if Anthropic doesn't stay in the lead position, then the real questions about the business model [emerge]. So the capex they have to spend is really real … So I would just say it's a much more complicated question. And there's a much wider range of outcomes — it's a more speculative bet than buying, for example, Visa, a company we own."

articles.title_orig: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing' that relies on personal data
articles.title_zh: NYC Council passes ban on 'surveillance pricing' that relies on personal data
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
The City Council passed a bill Thursday that bans companies in New York City from using surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
Surveillance pricing means shoppers see a price based on their personal data like demographics, credit, browsing history or purchasing history. The bill prohibits surveillance pricing both online and in stores, although the practice is mainly used on the web.
Speaker Julie Menin described surveillance pricing as an “insidious and predatory corporate practice” that erodes privacy and fairness.
“It's a practice that worsens the affordability crisis, and today it's a practice that we are going to be ending,” she said during a press conference ahead of the vote.
In one investigation cited by the Council, Target shoppers saw a jump in pricing based on location data showing whether they were inside or outside a store. Shoppers found that a 55-inch SmartTV cost $499 on the Target app when inside a store, and $599 when in the store parking lot.
Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing. Many of the companies have denied using the practice.
Under the bill, the city would be able to issue fines of up to $1,000 for each transaction that violates the ban.
Menin’s proposal follows legislation approved by Albany lawmakers in June that prohibits surveillance pricing online and in stores, with some exceptions.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement that he supports the ban. He called surveillance pricing “just another way corporations are finding to squeeze working people.”
“New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against their own pocketbooks,” he added.
Business groups have warned that the ban could hinder discounts or loyalty programs for customers.
“If enacted, this law will make it harder for small restaurants with limited marketing budgets to reach customers, putting them at a disadvantage against national chains,” said Josh Gold, a spokesperson for Uber.
The company operates Uber Eats, which allows restaurants to offer discounts based on search history and previous orders.
Menin said the legislation would not affect discounts.

articles.title_orig: US Wholesale Inflation Picks Up to Fastest Pace Since 2022
articles.title_zh: US Wholesale Inflation Picks Up to Fastest Pace Since 2022
articles.content_orig:
Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.
The producer price index , which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.
Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.
On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.
The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting, Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.
Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.
Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.
The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.
However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.
"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.
Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.
"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."
Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.
Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.
Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."
Other items in the PPI report also showed multiyear gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

Good morning, Space Fans, it is launch day for SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 and the world's largest rocket is now hours away from attempting its first double landing test flight. Liftoff remains on target for today, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT) from SpaceX's Starbase launch site in South Texas. You'll be able to w atch the Starship Flight 15 launch on this page, as well as on Space.com's homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace . Our live webcast will begin at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT) .
Last night, SpaceX rolled the Ship 42 upper stage out to the Starship launch pad and stacked it atop its Super Heavy booster. The Ship's number was accompanied by a fun sci-fi message - "Don't Panic" - in a nod to the Hitchhiker's Guide To The Galaxy books by Douglas Adams. Elon Musk's Tesla bore the same message when SpaceX launched it into space on the first Falcon Heavy mission.
Space.com's Josh Dinner is on site at Starbase and will be providing updates as possible from Starbase, which we'll share here as they're received.
Here's an update from Josh from the launch pad:
A post shared by Space.com (@spacedotcom)
SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 is the 15th test flight of Starship, the world's largest and most powerful rocket. SpaceX has designed the rocket to be fully reusable, and has landed its massive Super Heavy first stage booster several times.
Flight 15 is SpaceX's first attempt to land both the Super Heavy booster and its Ship upper stage by returning them to their launch pad and catching them in the pad's metal "Chopstick" arms. The landings will be about 22 hours apart, with Super Heavy landing minutes after launch and the Ship upper stage returning to Starbase on Saturday afternoon.
We'll be updating this page throughout the day with news from Josh, SpaceX and Starbase for this unprecedented 22.5-hour test flight. Here's our full timeline for SpaceX Starship Flight 15 .

Because the mission will last 22.5 hours, Starship will likely be visible in the night sky to stargazers hoping to see the giant spacecraft in orbit. Space.com's Skywatching Writer Anthony Wood has a great guide on how to see Starship in the night sky.
"When it passes overhead, it will look like a bright, fast-moving star crossing the sky — similar to the International Space Station , but potentially even brighter depending on its orientation," our skywatching columnist Joe Rao told Wood.

Liftoff is currently targeted for tomorrow (Nov. 13), during a 75-minute window opening at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT).
This flight could be a historic one for SpaceX and the space industry. For the first time, SpaceX will attempt to catch both stages of its massive Starship rocket — Super Heavy just minutes after launch, and the Ship upper stage roughly 22 hours later, following several orbits around Earth.
I'll be covering the action from here in Texas, so stay tuned to Space.com for updates as we count down to liftoff!

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.content_orig:
LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV made a triumphant return Friday to the Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for eight years and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto.”
Leo arrived in a plane decorated with “#LeoXFliesHome” stickers and he was greeted with a sign at the airport bearing the same message. A small dance troupe performed before him as he stepped off the plane.
He will stay in the area until Sunday to lead eight events, including a private dinner with the priests who once reported to him as bishop.
The crowds greeting Leo in Peru’s fourth largest city will likely be smaller than the estimated 3 million or so who welcomed the pope when he arrived Wednesday in Lima, the country’s capital.
But their enthusiasm more than made up for their smaller numbers as the former Bishop Robert Prevost of Chiclayo returned to this coastal city of nearly 700,000 as the leader of the  Catholic Church.
As toured in an open-air popemobile at the Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert plain just outside Chiclayo, the crowd erupted in cheers, many waving waved white-and-yellow Vatican flags.
Some had been waiting since last night to catch a glimpse of the pontiff, many of them forced to walk as lines of cars had blocked the roads where vendors sold hats, mini pope dolls and sweet Peruvian bread.
Maria Esther Chozo Reyes, 76, said she had taken a 12-hour bus ride from Lima and arrived Thursday afternoon before she camped overnight. “He knows the people of Chiclayo and he’s lived here, he’s made his mission here,” she told The Associated Press. “We really need his blessing.”
Thanking the people for their love and support, in his sermon Leo said it was a blessing to be in his former home.
“As I look at your faces, a prayer ⁠of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said, adding that his lung cancer disgnosis and surgery to remove part of one lung exactly a month ago had been a time of trial.
Leo’s sojourn to Chiclayo is midway through the final leg of his 12-day visit to South America , a historic trip that included stops in Argentina and Uruguay. And it’s the most sentimental part of his journey.
For while Leo was born in Chicago and English is his mother tongue, the first words he uttered from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica was a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved Diocese of Chiclayo.”
During his time in that city, Leo often repeated a joke: “Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter.”
Setting aside the fact that it’s actually two letters, Leo quickly became a beloved figure in Chiclayo by championing social justice issues, embracing the poor and venturing into the local prison to say Mass.
During the pandemic, Leo endeared himself to many by launching a fundraising drive to raise money for a badly-needed oxygen production plant.
When Cyclone Maku hit the area in March 2023, Leo was photographed wading through the floodwaters to get supplies to the destitute and distributing food at soup kitchens.
At Christmastime, Leo would drive a pickup truck laden with gifts into remote villages around Chiclayo and join family celebrations.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary, priest and finally as a bishop in Peru and became a citizen in 2015. During his two decades in the country, he was also a strident critic of then- Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori’s authoritarian regime .
On Thursday, Leo delivered a speech while sitting beside Fujimori’s daughter, recently-elected Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional performing arts center.
Leo urged the country’s leaders to cultivate honesty and integrity to strengthen public trust --- and called on officeholders to listen to their constituents.
“Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said.
There was thunderous applause when Leo referred to Peru as “my homeland.”
And Leo appeared to have tears in his eyes as he sang the Peruvian national anthem along with a children’s choir.
Claudio Lavanga reported from Lima and Corky Siemaszko from New York.
Claudio Lavanga is Rome-based foreign correspondent for NBC News.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.title_zh: Commerce Secretary Lutnick agreed to testify on Nvidia's AI chip sales to China
articles.content_orig:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.
Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.
Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."
"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.
The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."
Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.
There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough
Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."
In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.
Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.
Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.
Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.
Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq turn lower as wholesale inflation rises, Nvidia stock falls
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq turn lower as wholesale inflation rises, Nvidia stock falls
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks fell Friday as a sell-off in chip stocks picked up, Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock continued to decline, and an annual reading of wholesale inflation came in hot.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) edged lower by 0.2%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) declined 0.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) fell 1.6%.
Stocks sank amid a series of tremors, from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stepping down to elevated oil prices and a sell-off in government bonds.
Nvidia stock turned lower again as the fallout from Huang's affairs continued to unfold, raising the stakes for the company's third quarter earnings next Tuesday. Investors are debating whether the controversy surrounding the chip giant's former leader implicates the wider artificial intelligence boom that Nvidia has played a central role in building.
Chipmaker sector stocks declined, with AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) sinking.
Oil prices were little changed, providing some relief after a spike in prices sparked Thursday's sell-off in bonds. As traders braced for an interest rate hike in December, the 10-year Treasury yield ( ^TNX ) reached as high as 5.17% on Friday, its highest level since October.
The setup has pressured bitcoin ( BTC ), with the world's largest cryptocurrency tumbling below $70,000 Friday for the first time in nearly three months.
In economic news, wholesale inflation rose 0.3% month over month in October, according to the producer price index. The reading was less than the 0.4% economists expected, but the annual rate of 6.5% highlighted persistent inflation pressures, which likely keeps the Federal Reserve on track to hike interest rates next month.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares were downgraded to Hold at HSBC on Friday amid the fallout from Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. The firm also cut its price target to $170 from $365.
Analyst Frank Lee said investor confidence has been "shaken" as the company's "leadership succession plan is unclear." He said the fundamentals remain intact, though long-term uncertainty has increased.
"AI demand remains strong and NVIDIA has procured enough supply to achieve the 70% y-o-y revenue growth it outlined last quarter," Lee wrote.
Still, Lee said the new CEO could face challenges in executing Nvidia's existing roadmap and shaping its evolving product strategy, as well as "maintaining the same pricing power with customers and the same bargaining power with suppliers."
Tightened export restrictions are another potential risk that could ultimately weigh on revenue and earnings.
"While the findings of the independent probe by NVIDIA and Congressional scrutiny remain to be seen, one possible outcome could be enhanced export restrictions," Lee wrote.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock slipped more than 4% on Friday as a sell-off in the semiconductor sector accelerated and investors digested the exit of Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chip heavyweight, following reports of multiple affairs. The stock is expected to close out the week in the red, slipping below the $4 trillion market cap threshold.
Shares of chipmaker peers AMD ( AMD ), Broadcom ( AVGO ) and Intel ( INTC ) dropped roughly 9%, 6% and 5%, respectively.
Storage maker Sandisk ( SNDK ) stock extended declines from the prior session, falling 9%. Shares of memory chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ) also tanked 5% and 6%, respectively.
Wall Street's fear gauge jumped Friday as investors grew more uncertain about the stock market amid broader inflation worries and the Nvidia ( NVDA ) tumult.
The Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX ( ^VIX ), climbed above 20 in morning trading, extending a muted rise on Thursday as the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 were mixed.
The latest jump marks a sharp reversal from earlier this week, when volatility expectations retreated following last week's post-election market turmoil. The VIX surged nearly 70% on Nov. 5, one of its largest daily increases this year.
The index, which tracks expectations for S&P 500 volatility over the next 30 days, has averaged roughly 18.2 in 2026, according to Yahoo Finance data. Its recent swings underscore how quickly investors' appetite for risk has shifted.
Still, stocks are holding on to gains for the week.
Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports:
Richemont stock opened more than 4% lower on Friday morning as the Swiss luxury group reported slower growth in its jewelry business.
The owner of Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels posted first-half net profit of 2.5 billion euros (approximately $2.76 billion), up from 1.8 billion euros ($2 billion) a year earlier and above analyst forecasts of 2.26 billion euros ($2.5 billion).
But eyes were on jewelry, the group's growth engine, where sales rose 14%, short of the 16% analysts had expected, according to an RBC poll.
Many luxury brands have struggled amid foreign conflicts, rising gold prices, and cost-sensitive consumers. The luxury sector has fallen some 30% in 2026, per Barron's.
Wholesale inflation data came in better than expected for the month of October, but the long-term trend painted a worrying picture of rising prices.
The Producer Price Index, a measure of wholesale inflation, rose 0.3% month over month in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Friday. Economists had expected PPI to increase 0.4%.
However, over the last 12 months, the index for final demand increased 6.5% in October, the largest annual increase since November 2022.
That keeps the pressure on the Fed to raise interest rates next month.
Fed governor Michelle Bowman said Tuesday that rate hikes may be needed to slow the pace of price increases, Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger reported.
"Inflation pressures have persisted for longer than I had hoped and have shown recent signs of broadening," Bowman said in a speech in Washington.
US stocks opened higher on Friday as investors looked to close out a volatile week marked by rising Treasury yields, renewed pressure from oil prices and turmoil at Nvidia.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 0.4%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) was flat.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) shares rose 2% as investors continued to assess the fallout from Jensen Huang's departure ahead of the chipmaker's earnings next week. Other semiconductor stocks remained under pressure.
Investors were also watching the 10-year Treasury yield, which climbed to 5.10% Thursday.
The bull market won't have it easy in 2027, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports. According to Goldman Sachs strategist Kamakshya Trivedi, the vibes around AI investments are weakening.
Here's what Trivedi had to say about risks to stocks:
"Although we expect solid AI investment growth to continue, our forecasts imply that the investment growth impulse — additional AI investment as a share of GDP — will peak in early 2027. From a macro perspective, this should be a manageable event. But it may be a bigger test for markets for three reasons."
"First, the AI impulse has been a much larger contributor to growth in earnings and market value than to growth in GDP," Trivedi explained.
"Second, AI-related equities have taken credit for significant macro productivity gains, especially companies benefiting directly from the infrastructure boom, that have made them more vulnerable to any signs that we are on a less optimistic path," Trivedi added.
"Third, the point at which growth rates peak (a "second derivative" turning point) often matters, even if underlying growth rates (the "first derivative") remain healthy. Moving through that peak allows markets to place limits on the upside of an uncertain distribution and, as growth decelerates, the period of positive surprises to expectations often ends too, as we may be starting to see for the AI capex cycle."
Cerebras Systems ( CBRS ) stock jumped 13% in premarket trading after the AI chipmaker reported record third quarter revenue and raised its full-year outlook.

articles.title_orig: The Fed chief said AI would tame inflation. His colleagues disagree.
articles.title_zh: The Fed chief said AI would tame inflation. His colleagues disagree.
articles.content_orig:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.
"I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility," the policymaker said during an interview on "Squawk Box."
His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index , considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.
With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," he said.
"Inflation is rising. It's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we're adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it's starting to spread out of its lane," Goolsbee added.
Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week's inflation data.
Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.
"It's it's all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?" he said. "My feeling is, right now we're not."

articles.content_orig:
After years of waiting, gamers will finally be able to dive into GTA 6 next week, on November 19. Rockstar has already revealed plenty of details about the upcoming title, which is shaping up to be one of the biggest video game launches in history. However, while players will be able to enjoy the single-player campaign at launch, the game won't arrive with a multiplayer mode. But now, it seems that the release window for GTA 6 Online may have leaked.
Back in August, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier claimed that Take-Two and Rockstar weren't planning to reveal details about the new GTA Online anytime soon. He later clarified that Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick hadn't specifically discussed when the multiplayer mode would launch.
Interestingly, Bloomberg Originals has now published a new video titled "Why GTA 6 Took 13 Years and $1 Billion to Make," featuring Schreier and other Bloomberg reporters. While the video mainly discusses the game's lengthy development, the narrator makes an interesting claim about its multiplayer mode.
"The game that ships in 2026 is not even its final form. The real long-term engine arrives a year later with multiplayer," the narrator says. This suggests that GTA 6 Online could launch sometime in late 2027, roughly a year after the base game's release.
However, it's important to keep in mind that Rockstar and Take-Two haven't officially confirmed this release window. It's also unclear whether the narrator accidentally mentioned an unannounced detail or simply made an assumption about the multiplayer mode's arrival.
