articles.title_orig: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
articles.title_zh: Would You Get Stoned With The Scythians?
articles.content_orig:
9:00 AM EST on November 13, 2026
It's just like they told you it would happen in D.A.R.E.: You have been miraculously, tragically transported 2,800 years back in time, in the land that is now the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia. The site will be eventually called Tunnug 1 by the archaeologists who excavate it in 2017. But that is the future, and this is the present, meaning 800 B.C. You have come to sit with the Scythians, nomads who roamed the Eurasian steppes on horseback. You have even glimpsed their warrior-king, whose long and stately braids make him seem like a pretty cool guy. Also, he's smoking. Suddenly the warrior-king glimpses you back, his reddish eyes glinting in the firelight. He leans over to you, whispers something inscrutable in an Eastern Iranic language, and extends in his grizzled hands an ancient joint, leaving you with only one question: Would you smoke that shit?
There are, to be certain, pros and cons. But one thing is clear, per a paper published recently in the journal Science : The Scythians were definitely using cannabis to get high. The analysis, led by Fabio-haired University of Bern archaeologist Gino Caspari, represents the earliest definitive evidence of humans consuming marijuana as a psychoactive drug, which was previously only traced back 2,500 years ago where Sogdian mourners once lit up in the ancient Jirzankal Cemetery in what is now western China.
It's only fitting that marijuana hails from one of the highest places in the world: the eastern Tibetan Plateau, also known as the Roof of the World. The plant evolved around 28 million years ago, and as early as 4,000 years ago Chinese farmers cultivated the plant for rope, clothing, and paper, per Science . But it is harder to tell when in the archaeological record ancient people first became gone off that loud. Wild weed, the ancestors of the domesticated kind, has only a little tetrahydrocannabinol, or THC, the plant's intoxicating compound. Some researchers confirmed this when they tried to smoke wild weed and felt nothing, also per Science . (It is unclear if these particular researchers are also the paper's authors, who described cannabis as an "illicit" substance.)
But scholars have long suspected that Scythians were hotboxing, quite literally, in part due to the testimony of the Greek historian and geographer Herodotus, who was known to sensationalize his accounts (he once wrote of dog-sized ants that harvested gold). Herodotus recorded the following description of the nomads' funerary practices, per this translation of The Histories by George Campbell Macaulay:
The Scythians then take the seed of this hemp and creep under the felt coverings, and then they throw the seed upon the stones which have been heated red-hot: and it burns like incense and produces a vapour so thick that no vapour-bath in Hellas would surpass it: and the Scythians being delighted with the vapour-bath howl like wolves.
Let's go back to the warrior-king for a second. It's true that we don't know for sure if he's a warrior-king, but he would become one of the people buried at the center of the royal burial mound at Tunnug 1, whose tombs contained gold jewelry, statues of animals, weapons, and, most importantly, nearly a thousand whole cannabis seeds that appear to have been deposited around 2,800 years ago. This is where the archaeologists found strands of human hair, which had been preserved in two pristine braids. When they tested the hair, they found traces of cannabinol, or CBN, which is a byproduct of THC. Archaeology is almost always accompanied by some degree of uncertainty, but this mound of evidence—weed seeds and weed in hair—makes the case for stoner Scythians fairly open-and-shut.
Some outside researchers are skeptical, including forensic toxicologist Volker Auwärter, who told the AP that he found the hair analysis "scientifically weak," as well as a commenter called Fabio who wrote, "Drugs of choice back then was opium." But many scientists appear to be convinced, such as William Taylor, an archaeologist at the University of Colorado Boulder. "It’s easy to look at this stuff and say, ‘Oh, the Scythians toked the reefer,'" Taylor told Scientific American . "But in fact, it is a tremendously powerful snapshot into an interconnected world in which the people and cultures of the steppe were starting to shape life on both ends of a massive continent."
Tremendously powerful snapshots, sure, but let's return to the fact that the Scythians toked the reefer. I feel an important question that has been lost amid the buzz of the discovery: What would it be like get smoked out by the Scythians? I've taken the liberty of gathering some pros and cons.
Option 1: 420 B.C. Blaze It
If you were transported all the way back in time to 800 B.C. and offered a joint by a Scythian warrior-king, there are many good reasons to take at least one puff. You could imagine the punishment that might follow refusing a king. It might be nice to take the edge off 2,800 years of time travel. But the most important, I think, is that it would be real loser shit to say no.
But more seriously. The Scythians were famous for their " animal style ," which is not the ancestor of an In-N-Out secret menu item—which I'm sure a smoking Scythian would have loved—but rather a stylized artistic tradition that rendered highly stylized animals in gold, bronze, and bone. What kind of altered mental state might produce such a fantastic deer?
Imagine the small talk you could have with a roving band of Scythians. Sure, they spoke a group of ancient Iranic languages that you would probably not understand. Perhaps they would have spoken of their gods, such as the hearth-goddess Tabití . Perhaps they would have told you how to find one of the rivers on the steppe, such as the Borysthénēs , where you could find some kapa , or fish. You would smile and nod to all of this if you were high. Then maybe they would have offered you some cheese called hippákē .
If Herodotus is to be believed, smoking with a Scythian would probably not have involved a joint or a pipe, but rather a communal inhalation of smoke. But Herodotus makes this sound like a real good time. I, too, would like to throw the hemp seed upon the red-hot stones and howl like a wolf at the delights of the vapor-bath! Because the weed was found inside the burial mound, the researchers suspect that it may have played a role in a ritual funerary practice, perhaps for some kind of religious experience. But there is another, more sinister reason the Scythians may have wanted you to, in Taylor's particular parlance, toke the reefer.
Option 2: Say No To Scythians
Although the wooden tombs of Tunnug 1 contained the graves of important individuals buried in coffins made of tree trunks and logs, these wooden structures were topped with what is often called a "spectral cavalcade," a fancy word for a heap of sacrificed horses and humans. Horses, sure, but humans? We must return once more to our friend Herodotus, who described in great detail the spectral cavalcade practice that follows a king's burial in The Histories :
Afterwards, when the year comes round again, they do as follows:—they take the most capable of the remaining servants,—and these are native Scythians, for those serve him whom the king himself commands to do so, and his servants are not bought for money,—of these attendants then they strangle fifty and also fifty of the finest horses; and when they have taken out their bowels and cleansed the belly, they fill it with chaff and sew it together again.
On the horses they put bridles and bits, and stretch the bridles tight in front of them and then tie them up to pegs: and of the fifty young men who have been strangled they mount each one upon his horse, having first run a straight stake through each body along by the spine up to the neck; and a part of this stake projects below, which they fasten into a socket made in the other stake that runs through the horse. articles.title_orig: Why Social Security’s annual COLA matters more as retirees get older
articles.title_zh: Why Social Security’s annual COLA matters more as retirees get older
articles.content_orig:
Bill Sweeney, AARP's senior vice president of government affairs, on the Social Security COLA for 2027.
The Social Security Administration (SSA) revealed last month the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, which will give a boost to beneficiaries' monthly checks amid stubborn inflation.
The COLA will boost benefit checks by 3.6% in 2027, starting with payments distributed for January. That increase will amount to an average benefit boost of $75 per month for typical beneficiaries.
Each year, the COLA is computed to account for inflation that occurred in the third quarter of the preceding year, and this year's inflation data from the months of July, August and September led to the 3.6% increase.
Bill Sweeney, senior vice president of government affairs at AARP, spoke with FOX Business and said that for the "vast majority of Americans, their Social Security is kind of the only thing in their retirement portfolio that is inflation-adjusted, and so it becomes really important for retirees, especially as they get older."
SOCIAL SECURITY ANNOUNCES COST-OF-LIVING ADJUSTMENT FOR 2027
Social Security's annual COLA for 2027 will be 3.6%. (Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)
Sweeney said that the COLA is particularly important for older retirees to allow their budgets to keep pace with prices.
"This cost-of-living adjustment – it may not matter as much when you're 67 or 68 – but as you get into your 70s and 80s when it's no longer realistic for you to go back to work if you need to sort of fill in your budget, the COLA really does make sure that Social Security keeps up with rising costs," he said.
SOCIAL SECURITY CHIEF BISIGNANO SAYS PROGRAM WILL 'BE AROUND FOR ANOTHER 90 YEARS'
Social Security and private savings play a crucial role in retirement savings given the decline in pensions. (Mark Felix/The Washington Post)
Historically, pension plans were a bigger part of Americans' financial outlook, but as those have declined in recent decades, private savings and Social Security benefits are playing an increasingly important role in retirement planning.
"We used to talk about a three-legged stool of retirement security , which was your pension, your private savings and Social Security," Sweeney said. "The Gen Xers are the first generation really retiring with only those two stool legs left."
He said that "about half of people rely on Social Security for almost all of their income," adding that "about 20%, almost all of their income is Social Security, and so this COLA is really important for this group, especially for whom this is the difference between putting food on the table or not."
ONE TYPE OF SOCIAL SECURITY ADJUSTMENT COULD CUT THE 75-YEAR SHORTFALL IN HALF
Social Security's annual COLA boosts benefits for the following year when inflation rises in the current year. (Getty Images/stock)
The 2027 COLA will be the largest since 2023, when benefits got an 8.7% boost to account for the spike in inflation that had occurred.
As inflation eased in the past three years, the COLA shrank accordingly and came in at 3.2% in 2024, 2.5% in 2025 and 2.8% in 2026.
"Social Security's cost-of-living adjustment is really critical to making sure that in years of high inflation, you don't fall behind," Sweeney said.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Israeli spy chief in D.C. as Netanyahu presses Trump to resume war
articles.content_orig:
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.
That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.
And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.
But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?
Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.
However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.
In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.
Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.
“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.
“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.
Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.
“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.
On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.
“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.
That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.
On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.
According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.
The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.
Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.
The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.
There would be serious divisions.
“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.
But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.
Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.
“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.
Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”
“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.
Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.
“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.
Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.
But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.
Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.
In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.
While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister .
Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly , killing about 1,400 Palestinians.

articles.title_orig: Watch CNBC's full interview with Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent on Nvidia, China trade
articles.title_zh: Watch CNBC's full interview with Treasury Sec. Scott Bessent on Nvidia, China trade
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal.
But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."
The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.
Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.
Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.
Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."
But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."
"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.
Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.
This is breaking news. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Neocloud Nscale Reveals $5.5 Billion Debt and Closer Nvidia Ties Ahead of IPO
articles.title_zh: Neocloud Nscale Reveals $5.5 Billion Debt and Closer Nvidia Ties Ahead of IPO
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia -backed neocloud Nscale on Thursday released updated paperwork for a U.S. initial public offering.
The company had a third-quarter net loss of $1.69 billion on $307.5 million in revenue, which was up 1,344% year over year, according to an updated prospectus for its planned initial public offering. The net loss widened from $1.02 billion in the second quarter, when the company generated $140.6 million in revenue, up 1,252%.
London-based Nscale filed to go public in September , but hasn't updated its prospectus since then. The company did not specify how much it intends to raise in the public offering on the New York Stock Exchange.
Since then the company has faced public setbacks.
Microsoft walked away from an Nscale data center that it had planned to use in England. Darren Hardman, Microsoft's CEO for the U.K and Ireland, told CNBC in October that the decision had to do with Nscale's ability to get access to electricity.
The Financial Times reported that Microsoft decided against renewing a contract with Nscale in Texas. The company said in its IPO filing that it expects Microsoft to be a "significant customer in future periods."
The neocloud market, which focuses on renting access to chips such as Nvidia graphics processing units to clients, has been in tumult, partly because Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday, after admitting to being unfaithful to his wife. Nvidia is investigating Huang's relationship with a woman whom intelligence agencies have called a Chinese spy.
In October investors pressured shares of Nscale rival CoreWeave, but the stock advanced almost 25% on Wednesday on strong results. CoreWeave pulled back about 7% on Thursday following the departure of Huang, who has overseen investments in the neocloud.
Shares of another neocloud, Nebius , fell about 17% on Thursday, with the company issuing light full-year guidance.
But Nscale can point to growing business with Anthropic, which itself is aiming to go public. In late September Anthropic exercised its right to contract for additional computing power at an Nscale site in West Virginia.

articles.title_orig: From Jensen Huang to Elon Musk: The uniforms of tech bros and the meaning behind them
articles.title_zh: From Jensen Huang to Elon Musk: The uniforms of tech bros and the meaning behind them
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
W e all thought the AI bubble had burst in China, then Jensen Huang had an affair. Except, oops, it was two alleged affairs. And Donald Trump knew about at least one of them, apparently, but who doesn’t cheat on their wives and what damage can a woman really do?
Now that Jensen Huang has finally “resigned” (presumably been ousted) from Nvidia, it’s probably time to discuss how damaging such a belief system is — not for someone’s soul, but for national security. Because Trump’s blind spots, and the blind spots of the fools around him, allowed for a situation that made absolutely everybody vulnerable in an industry the US was supposed to “win”.
Trump’s first reaction to hearing that Huang was likely having an affair with a Chinese spy — an allegation that was shared with him by US intelligence, months ago — was, apparently, to ignore it. His second reaction, this week, when Huang’s affairs started making headlines, was to say that he thought Huang should stay on as CEO, that he’s a good guy and that it doesn’t feel like a big deal.
Needless to say: it is a huge deal. It’s not just a huge deal because we now know Huang was somewhat of a tomcat, also apparently sleeping with one of his direct reports in the company. It’s a huge deal because it shows how much those all-important AI capabilities — the industry Trump is determined to “win” at; the industry he was against putting any guardrails in for, because something-something China — are controlled by a handful of extremely fallible men. Although this fact has become obvious to everyone, and has hit the stock market hard , those men still refuse to accept that that’s a problem. Case in point: Elon Musk publicly offering to hire Huang when it became clear that the CEO would actually have to go.
Trump believes in a back-slapping, boys’-club business world that doesn’t exist anymore. As we know, he loves a ceremony where he can slap on a hard hat and sign a beam. He loves talking about pipes and granite outside the Reflecting Pool. He does not seem to understand how catastrophic it is that Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, whose Singapore-based business Megaspeed appears to have helped Nvidia chips make their way into China via Singapore.
But “he had no idea the person he was talking to was a spy,” said Trump, as if that isn’t entirely the point of spying. It’s also worth underlining that if you believe women are dispensable, naive fools, you won’t have the imagination to grasp how extremely clever women spies operate, and how extremely dangerous they can be to your national security.
What Trump can’t grasp is that this isn’t about what Jensen Huang believed or knew or whether he’s a nice guy who can build some nice factories again in the future. And of course he’d rather believe his own narrative. Huang helped fund Trump’s infamous ballroom, to the tune of $25 millio n. He had phone calls with Trump about AI. He travelled on Air Force One. He also sold the president a vision of the future where Nvidia computer chips transformed the AI landscape and totally reshaped the economy in every way.
Huang’s perspective on China was an interesting one, too. He wanted open trade with China and he argued that Nvidia should compete with them in an open market manner, rather than trying to seal off trade secrets. He thought the US should try and compete for the massive, highly lucrative Chinese market rather than leaving it to smaller Chinese competitors. Democrats wanted to speak to him in Congress about that (he never turned up.) And now it raises some questions: Sure, the chips guy wanted to sell chips to more people and make lots of money. But how much of that viewpoint was informed by conversations he was having with Alice?
Now we’ve heard rumors that Huang was also having an affair with an executive at Nvidia, we have to wonder whether his behavior wasn’t more of an open secret. And even if one of your affair partners isn’t allegedly working for China, you’re still a security risk if you’re putting it about like that.
Trump has created his own little oligarchy in AI. Tech billionaires cycle in and out of the White House, contributing funds to his little renovation projects, having cosy little dinners with him at Mar-a-Lago. There are only a handful of American companies that have built LLMs and they are eating up smaller companies in the space at a rapid rate. They also help choose and fund the next companies downstream, or have very close relationships with the firms that do so.
This network includes the president’s family: Donald Trump Jr is a partner at a company that invests in AI companies, including Musk’s xAI and Vulcan Elements, which currently has a $620 million loan with the Pentagon . Junior also has a data center business with his brother, Eric. And Eric has interests in companies that use AI for defense and robotics, including a company that has a Marine Corps contract . That’s without going into any of the other administration officials, friends and advisors who also have their fingers in a lot of AI pies.
We now have ourselves a situation where there is an enormous concentration of AI infrastructure in a handful of companies, increasingly speculative investment assumptions and a political system in which the interests of major technology executives are closely intertwined with government decision-making. And so far, we’ve also had a president who completely resisted any legal oversight or guardrails around AI development, even as polling shows that’s what everyday Americans want. No wonder Trump’s meetings with Xi Jinping have been so friendly.
So it turns out Trump isn’t just bad at judging people, but he’s also bad for American businesses, and that he isn’t just bad for American businesses, but he’s also bad for national security. The ideology he and his MAGA acolytes espouse is actively damaging to the country. Because the thing about diversity is that it isn’t just a buzzword; it offers multiple layers of defense. If all your biggest business ventures are controlled by a bunch of men with the same personalities and the same friends, you’re extremely vulnerable to attack from outsiders. They don’t have to spend much time and effort trying to work out how to pick each one of you off, because you’re all the same. Homogeneity breeds groupthink; groupthink breeds weakness.
All that posturing about “dominating the western hemisphere” means nothing if you’re too blinded by your feelings to make logical decisions. And essentially this has always been the problem with MAGA: lots of foot-stomping, lots of rage, lots of empty words about taking back the country, and then a lot of nonsense in the background that damages the economy and puts America into a vulnerable position.
Democrats will now have a chance to push pending legislation around AI and data chips while showing how truly dumb Trump, Musk and all his billionaire buddies have been to the public. This is complex, fiddly, technological stuff but communicating it concisely to a busy populace will be key to them succeeding in Congress.
Trump is fond of complaining that “the world was laughing at us” before he became president. The truth is that everyone’s laughing at the leather jackets and the lapses of judgment now. And Democrats need to get the word out in a way that even Donald Trump could understand.

articles.title_orig: Germany's Merz asks Trump for 'no surprises' from Putin talks
articles.title_zh: Germany's Merz asks Trump for 'no surprises' from Putin talks
articles.content_orig:
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow Thursday to discuss Ukraine, after two days of U.S.-led talks between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi yielded no major breakthroughs.
“I think progress was made. I think it was made earlier today,” Witkoff told reporters after the meeting at the Senate Palace of the Kremlin. “People didn't think that we were going to restart trilateral. We’ve restarted it. We’ve set a new meeting. This is what President [Donald] Trump wants to see."
He went on to say that a European representative would be present for the next stage of the talks, which are set to look at the continent’s wider security arrangements. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he said.
Witkoff and Kushner are now en route to Dublin, where they are set to brief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on any developments from the talks. Zelensky is among the dozens of world leaders in the Irish capital for the European Political Community summit.
Zelensky has expressed optimism about the next round of negotiations, saying there is a "window of opportunity” to reach a peace deal with Russia.
“There really is this window of opportunity, when all the participants involved in this negotiating process could get the result by the beginning of 2027,” he said , speaking alongside Irish Taoiseach (Prime Minister) Micheál Martin during a press conference in Dublin.
Although Russian and Ukrainian negotiators ⁠reported some progress during this week's Abu Dhabi talks—including a prisoner swap agreement—all sides have acknowledged that significant differences remain, particularly over territory.
Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the entirety of the eastern Donbas. With negotiations over territory deadlocked, U.S. mediators instead sought to steer discussions toward post-war security guarantees and reconstruction.
However, Putin doubled down on his opposition to the idea of foreign peace-keeping troops being stationed in Ukraine if an agreement is reached, telling Witkoff and Kushner it would be considered by Russia as a "continuation of war."
Fully integrating European representatives into future negotiations could also prove challenging, despite Witkoff's confidence on the matter. Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who led Russia's delegation in Abu Dhabi, previously expressed skepticism over any European involvement.
Yuri ⁠Ushakov, Putin's foreign policy adviser, ​ told reporters ⁠after the Moscow meeting that the Russian President will continue talks on Ukraine with Trump ‌at the Asian-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in ‌China later this month.
Despite the major obstacles that remain, Trump has expressed renewed optimism about ending the war—a goal he had previously claimed would be achieved on his first day back in office in 2025. “We're seeing a very strong inclination to end [the war between] Russia and Ukraine,” the President insisted during a press conference Monday.
The European Union is preparing a new sanctions package against Russia in an effort to increase economic pressure on Moscow and strengthen Ukraine's position in future peace talks.
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said the bloc was preparing its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, alongside a separate proposal to address Ukraine's financial needs, by the year-end.
“We are, as a Commission, preparing a proposal [on] how to cover the financial needs of Ukraine in 2027, we will come with the sanctions package and the proposal for the financial needs before the next European Council,” she told reporters in Dublin. “We will support Ukraine, be it at wartime, or be it at peacetime."
The next European Council meeting is scheduled to take place in Brussels across Nov. 26-27.
Other European leaders also took the opportunity to underscore the importance of bolstering Ukraine.
French President Emmanuel Macron said that “without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine,” insisting “there is no more U.S. support.”
In an address at the summit, Zelensky appealed to Europe to continue supporting Ukrainian territory and championed sanctions against Russia as an effective measure.
In a separate display of solidarity, the U.K. government announced new levies targeting Russia's 10 largest oil producers. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described the move as “a sweep of stinging new sanctions to turn the screws on Russia’s oil revenues and drive forward an end to the Kremlin’s needless war.”
Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, stand alongside Irish Taoiseach Micheal Martin, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and French President Emmanuel Macron at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Nov. 12, 2026. Brian Lawless—Getty Images
As Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky raised concerns about new speed restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade sister version of Elon Musk’s Starlink service.
Zelensky said the Ukrainian military was facing "systematic" restrictions to Starshield and, as a result, struggling to intercept Russian drones. "This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said . "We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side."
TIME has reached out to the White House and SpaceX for comment.
Starlink offers Internet connectivity from satellites in low-Earth orbit. Its sister service Starshield, a military version developed for the Pentagon, relies on the Starlink network and has become a vital component for Ukrainian forces, strengthening its far-reaching drone strike missions and air defenses.
Last month, Ukraine complained that speed restrictions had been imposed on Starshield, leading to the “ failure ” of several military missions. There were conflicting reports as to how the service came to be restricted.
Reuters, citing three U.S. officials, had reported that the decision to limit the service came from inside the White House.
When approached for comment, a senior U.S. official told TIME: “No such request was ever made by the President.”
When initially addressing the matter, SpaceX founder and CEO Musk emphasized how Starlink and Starshield are different. He cited the U.S. authorities as being in control of the latter’s usage determinations.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS,” he said on X. “Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company.”
Musk later said his company SpaceX had imposed limits on the use of its Starlink satellite system, accusing Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity. He denied being behind the simultaneous issue with Starshield.
Kyiv denied breaching Starlink’s terms of service. “It’s very strange that Elon Musk doesn’t know about the restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine,” said Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov via Telegram . “Starlink does not work over Russian territory. So we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and mid-range strikes.”

articles.title_orig: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
articles.title_zh: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
articles.content_orig:
A car explosion in southern Moscow injured a former aide to a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician on Friday, according to Russian authorities, the second apparent attack in two days.
Sergey Zavorotny, who served as an adviser to the former pro-Russian prime minister of Ukraine Mykola Azarov, was transported to a city hospital for medical care, the Investigative Committee of Russia for the city of Moscow said in a statement.
Azarov served as the Ukrainian prime minister from 2010 to 2014, when he fled to Russia during the street protests known as the Maidan Revolution .
The Russian Investigative Committee said that a comprehensive investigation into the explosion on Moscow’s Kirovogradskaya Street is underway.
Video from the scene shows a dark gray SUV that has been heavily damaged, with the windows apparently blown out.
It’s the latest in a series of apparent attacks or assassinations against political and military figures inside Russia. On Thursday, a car explosion in St. Petersburg killed a Russian serviceman, the local Investigative Committee said.
Russia has blamed Ukraine for earlier assassinations of military officials.
Ukrainian authorities have not commented on this week’s explosions.
The latest incidents come amid the United States’ latest diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week, and announced that European delegates will join the next round of peace talks .
The pair had flown to Moscow after trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week concluded with no clear breakthrough.
After speaking to Putin in Moscow, Kushner said: “Both sides have now agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include our European partners.”

articles.title_orig: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.title_zh: Alice Huang-Linked Firm Procured Banned Nvidia Chips in China
articles.content_orig:
Singapore, a hub for billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia sales each year, finds itself increasingly in the crosshairs of Washington's push to stop advanced AI chips from reaching China, as the chipmaker CEO's scandal once again thrusts the city-state into the spotlight.
The Southeast Asian nation said Thursday that it had barred Alice Huang, the businesswoman at the center of a scandal that catalyzed the end of Jensen Huang's run as Nvidia CEO, from re-entering the country.
A fifth person was handed 41 charges on Friday in a Singapore fraud case involving computer servers that might have contained Nvidia chips and were exported to Malaysia. The alleged transactions in the broader case totaled about $390 million, prosecutors said March last year.
The investigations into several companies and key officials, including Megaspeed International, began in February 2025 and remained ongoing as of Thursday.
Authorities have been examining whether servers exported through Singapore to Malaysia without entering the domestic market were subsequently rerouted to another destination, contrary to declarations made in Singapore, the Ministry of Home Affairs said in a statement late Thursday.
Singapore has faced growing international scrutiny, particularly from the U.S., over its role as a major billing and potential transit hub for Nvidia chips that U.S. officials say have reached China.
The U.S. has imposed export restrictions on Nvidia's most cutting-edge AI chips to China since 2022 to curb Beijing's surging AI development.
Nvidia's revenue linked to Singapore rose to 22% in the fiscal quarter ending July 2025, up from 8% in 2023, with the country's trade ministry estimating chips physically delivered there accounted for less than 1% of the chipmaker's revenue.
Experts have pointed to gaps in enforcement of U.S. export restrictions and Singapore's corporate system that make it hard to trace where advanced Nvidia chips ultimately end up.
Nvidia chips can be legally sold to customers in other countries, such as Malaysia or Singapore, and then illicitly resold or re-exported to China. Chinese companies can also legally gain remote access to the most advanced AI chips hosted in data centers outside China rather than buying the hardware directly.
Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at Council on Foreign Relations and former U.S. national security official, said that Southeast Asia has become "a major hub for chip smuggling and export control circumvention," importing tens of billions of dollars' worth of AI chips per year.
Singapore has stepped up efforts to police suspected chip diversion since last year, including investigations involving alleged fraud and money laundering.
Authorities acknowledged the potential "blind spots between separate monitoring of trade flows and banking flows," said Alvin Camba, lead scientist and director of research at Lyvi, an Austin-based AI risk assessment firm. Correlating physical shipments with related financial transactions can be "challenging," he added.
"Singapore's strong corporate secrecy regulations, which offer extensive protections for foreign investors, can also make it difficult to rapidly identify the true recipients of goods," Camba said.
Those challenges can be exploited to "obfuscate financial flows and potentially circumvent global restrictions on technology transfers," he added, urging constant adaptation from regulators.
Singapore said it had received limited help from U.S. authorities in its yearlong investigation.
Police sought information on Super Micro Computer Inc., a U.S. server supplier relevant to the probe, but the company provided limited cooperation, according to the Thursday statement.
The city-state first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025, and has repeated its request on several occasions since September last year. "Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company," it said.
Police interviewed Alice Huang, a Hong Kong resident who was then Megaspeed's CEO, chairperson and a key controller, in June 2025.
In February 2026, authorities concluded that there was insufficient evidence that she had committed offenses related to the declarations under investigation. She was nonetheless barred from re-entering Singapore after being found providing inaccurate information to downplay her role in Megaspeed.
The country does not enforce "unilateral export controls" imposed by other countries, the ministry said in Thursday's statement, but it expects companies operating there to take foreign export rules into account in their international business activities.
Megaspeed, which was spun off from a Chinese gaming company, became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer in less than three years and has bought more than $4.8 billion worth of its chips since June 2024, according to The New York Times, though the company has denied any wrongdoing.
Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese intelligence asset passing information to Beijing, served as managing director at Megaspeed for eight months in 2023 but has reportedly continued to play a leading role at the company.
Jensen Huang has resigned as Nvidia CEO on Thursday, ending 33 years at the helm after revelations that he had two extramarital affairs, plunging the chipmaker at the heart of the global AI boom into crisis.
Nvidia appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

articles.title_orig: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.title_zh: Widespread Microsoft Outage Roils Businesses, Governments and More
articles.content_orig:
Police forces, hospitals, GP surgeries and councils across the south of England have been sharing advice and updates after a global Microsoft outage left them without email access.
Most say they are continuing to operate as normal but some online forms and electronic-based services are not working and there may be delays to enquiries.
The region's three police forces - Hampshire & Isle of Wight, Thames Valley and Dorset - all said their phone lines were working and they were able to respond to emergencies but their online reporting systems were down.
Hospitals have asked outpatients to attend booked appointments, adding there was no need to check they were going ahead.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems" .
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues on Friday had so far been unsuccessful.
In a Facebook update on Friday morning, Dorset Police said: "We are currently unable to receive online form submissions. Until this is resolved, if your report is time-critical but not an emergency, please dial 101.
"If your report can wait until Microsoft restores its service, please submit an online form once you are able to do so."
Hampshire police sought to allay fears about the effect of the outage on services.
It said: "We can confirm that our ability to answer and respond to 999 and 101 calls has not been impacted by the widely reported issues with Microsoft.
"We know that the current situation will be causing concern... but our ability to respond to emergencies has not been compromised."
Isle of Wight NHS Trust said its emergency services remained operational through the outage and teams had "established plans in place to minimise disruption and maintain safe patient care".
It said: "If your enquiry is urgent, please contact the relevant service by telephone rather than email where possible."
Oxford University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust said: "Our services remain operational, but there may be delays in responding to enquiries.
"If you need to contact us, please telephone us rather than email.
"If you have an appointment with us, please attend as planned. There is no need to contact us to confirm your appointment."
Tower House GP surgery in Ryde said the outage could affect some of its services, with delays responding to online consultations, hospital letters and discharge documents.
It said it was prioritising urgent clinical matters and patient safety.
Slough Borough Council in Berkshire said staff at its customer service centre who usually dealt with email enquiries had been transferred onto the phones but urged people only to call if their request was urgent because lines were expected to be busy.
East Hampshire District Council said its emails were down but residents registered on its MyEHDC system could still use the general enquiries form.
Lyme Regis Town Council in Dorset said it was using a mobile phone number for urgent issues because its telephone lines were also affected and working intermittently.

articles.title_orig: Apple should have made the MacBook logo RGB
articles.title_zh: Apple should have made the MacBook logo RGB
articles.content_orig:
The PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.
The PROLED MacBook Pro’s logo is lit with boring white LEDs. Missed opportunity.
When Apple CEO John Ternus announced the first touchscreen Mac last month, the biggest reaction in the room wasn’t for the PROLED MacBook Pro ’s OLED touchscreen or the thinner and lighter chassis; it was for the illuminated lid logo. It’s a throwback to the light-up logos on the old MacBooks, which Apple started phasing out in 2015 , and which were completely gone by the 2018 MacBook Air redesign . It’s a nostalgia play, but boy did it work. It’s fun!
Just like in the old days, the new logo’s brightness is linked to the screen’s: The brighter or dimmer the screen, the brighter or dimmer the logo. But the light-up logo on the old MacBooks was illuminated by the screen’s backlight, and an OLED display doesn’t have one. Thanks to iFixit , we now know it’s lit by four white LEDs and synced with the screen’s brightness by software. But that means Apple could have used RGB LEDs.
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet, or anything in between? On the lid of your new MacBook Pro? Why not? After all, Apple insists it’s still serious about gaming , and nothing says “serious about gaming” like RGB lighting.
I was secretly hoping users would be able to customize the illuminated lid cutout much like the Xbox logo on Microsoft’s Elite Series 2 controllers . But alas, no luck. You can turn off the illumination with some Terminal commands or take control of it with a third-party app. But when it’s lit, it’s only lit with white light. And iFixit’s teardown also showed the difficulty of accessing those LEDs (the screen delaminated and broke in the process). So we’re unlikely to see LED RGB mods for it unless someone’s brave enough to void their warranty and risk a pricey screen repair on their $3,000 laptop.
The most fun you can have with the Apple lid logo is to install a free third-party app like LogoLight and have it pulse, breathe, match the beat of any music you’re playing, or flash some Morse code. There’s some fun there, but if you combined these features with a splash of color we’d really be cooking.
MacBooks aren’t gaming laptops, so RGB lighting may seem like a mismatch, but multicolor LEDs could have been a cool Easter egg. Nobody thought Apple would put a touchscreen on a MacBook either, and the iPhone Duo and HomeView also show Apple is in a new age of experimentation during the early Ternus era. Maybe if the light-up lid logo ever comes to future MacBook Airs or a MacBook Neo, Apple could cut loose a little.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang’s years-long effort to get close to China
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang’s years-long effort to get close to China
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.
Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.
Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.
"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.
The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.
Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.
On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.77%, nearly 6% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
Tech stocks slumped Thursday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 0.3% as markets digested the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Thursday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt  lingers.
It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.
Neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.
CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.75% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped 18% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.
It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.
"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.
"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday , before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."
"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."
Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.
The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.
"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."
— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.title_zh: How the Microsoft outage has been felt worldwide
articles.content_orig:
At least 74 countries have been affected by the Microsoft outage since it was detected after midday US Eastern Time (17:00 GMT) on Thursday.
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and artificial intelligence software Copilot, were experiencing "connectivity problems", the company said.
As of 12:00 GMT on Friday, it reported seeing "encouraging recovery progress in Europe" while Japan remained "comparatively more stable" and North America was "also improving".
From city governments in the US to Australian spy agencies, the disruption has been widespread. Here's what's been happening around the world.
In the US , staff with the House of Representatives told Politico their work had been halted by the outage.
"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.
Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.
The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.
"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."
In Canada , a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.
The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.
Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.
Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers may not be able to receive emails about their trips due to the outage.
Disruptions have also been reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.
In Japan , some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.
"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times .
The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.
Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".
Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.
In the Philippines , the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".
In India , the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.
People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.
"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.
Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.
Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.
China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.
Australia's spy and federal police agencies have been affected by the outage, though officials have suggested the impact is minimal.
"The impact that they are dealing with is very much on email system", the head of the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, Mike Burgess, told reporters.
Other Australian public service providers also confirmed they had been affected by the outage, but similarly said this was mostly limited to emails, and the BBC understands there were no major impacts across New South Wales' primary services in health, education, transport, and emergency services.
European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.
In the UK , GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.
Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.
A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.
"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."
Some parts of Asia, Europe and Africa remain unaffected, according to Downdetector. These include Russia, where the use of Microsoft applications is heavily restricted, or phased out in favour of domestic alternatives.
However, this could also be a case of under-reporting in some countries, where Downdetector is among the websites blocked due to censorship.

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills at least six people, officials say
articles.content_orig:
An Israeli airstrike on a hospital in southern Gaza overnight killed at least six people, the Health Ministry in the Palestinian enclave said Thursday.
The strike hit a surgery building at Nasser Hospital, with medical staff and patients among those killed, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, health officials said. The Israeli military said it was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants.
The strike — the latest despite an ongoing U.S.-backed ceasefire — shattered ceilings and left debris strewn across wards inside the hospital, which is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza after the destruction of Israel’s yearslong military assault.
Palestinian surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira was among those killed, the Health Ministry said. He was featured in the 2026 documentary “American Doctor,” which followed three American doctors helping to provide medical care in Gaza.
An array of munitions debris was displayed at the hospital site as media visited on Thursday. Two munitions experts said an image supplied to NBC News appeared to show debris from a GBU-39 Small Diameter Bomb. The U.S. is known to supply Israel with GBU-39 munitions, which are produced by Boeing in the United States and sold to a number of countries.
The IDF and Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether U.S.-manufactured munitions were used in the strike. While the image was captured at Nasser Hospital following the strike, NBC News is not able to independently confirm that they were the munitions used in the attack or how they came to be displayed there.
Justin Bronk, a senior research fellow for airpower and technology in the military sciences at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank based in London, said he made that determination based on the “wing section visible,” adding that the GBU-39 “is a U.S. supplied weapon.”
Brian Castner, a crisis researcher at Amnesty International, also identified the munitions as belonging to a GBU-39, adding that Israel has used the bomb “in many strikes in Gaza.”
Sam Lair, a fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute who manages and conducts investigations into nuclear and missile programs, said NBC News’ imagery appeared inconclusive, but “the wings, tail actuation system, lugs, and warhead” shown in other photos appear to match “a GBU-39 series small diameter bomb.”
“It looks to be some kind of glide bomb or cruise missile, and the English on the frame suggests it could be U.S.-origin, but I don’t see anything conclusive,” he said.
Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, head of the surgery department at Nasser Hospital, said there was no “notice, warning or anything” before the hospital was attacked. “Suddenly, there was fire and shelling and walls were brought down instantly,” he said.
He said he was not aware of any “resistance fighters or combatants present — only a medical team treating patients.”
NBC News also spoke with two surgeons who travelled to Gaza from the U.K. earlier this month to assist with medical care, and were said were in the hospital when the missile struck.
Both Dr. Goher Rahbour, a consultant general and colorectal surgeon, and Dr. Stephan Verborg, a limb reconstruction surgeon, said they were also not aware of any warning from the Israeli military before the strike, which hit the hospital shortly after midnight.
“I heard the impact and I felt the explosion because the whole hospital shook,” Verborg said in a phone interview Thursday. He said he was about 15 to 20 meters away from the point of impact, adding: “You could smell the smoke. You could see the dust.”
Rahbour said he had been operating with Abu Shaira, whom he described as a “lovely” and “affable” person, earlier that day. He said they had been laughing and joking together Wednesday evening in the hours just before the Palestinian surgeon was killed.
Both doctors had traveled to Gaza early this month through the organization IDEALS, a U.K. charity seeking to provide sustainable humanitarian aid to regions affected by conflict or natural disasters. They said they had not seen any indication of a Hamas presence in the hospital.
Tributes were paid to Abu Shaira. “Dr. Rizq was at the hospital during the entire war,” Dr. Mohammed Zaqout, director general of the Health Ministry in Gaza, could be seen telling a crowd of mourners, surrounding a body covered in a shroud, in a video captured for NBC News on Thursday. “He didn’t abandon his duties for even one day.”
Nasser Hospital said a 13-year-old boy, identified as Jihad Naeem Muhammad Abu Tilikh, was also among those killed.
The Israeli military and the Israel Security Agency said they struck a senior Hamas member, along with other militants, who they said had “advanced” attacks from the hospital in the southern Gaza Strip overnight. In a later statement, they identified the senior member as Muhammad Abu Ismail, who they said served as the commander of Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade and had also been responsible for holding hostages in Gaza.
The IDF and ISA said Hamas had “established a presence within the hospital complex and used it as a command center” and stored weapons and conducted interrogations and torture from within the medical complex.
The IDF claimed the hospital’s second floor “serves as a Hamas military HQ, where civilians are not permitted to enter,” alleging that “dozens of hostages were held captive” there earlier in the war. It shared undated photos of weapons that it alleged were found within the complex and others.
The IDF and ISA said steps had been taken to “mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.” They also later said “advance warnings were issued to the population.” The IDF said it was looking into reports that medical workers,  including Abu Shaira, and patients were killed.
One woman, Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza, said her brother, Khaled Abu Anza, was killed in the strike, with Nasser Hospital separately confirming his death.
A number of media outlets, including Israeli media outlet Ynet , reported that a commander in Hamas’ Khan Younis Brigade of that same name was killed in the strike. Asked to confirm that and whether he was directly targeted, the IDF said it would get back on the matter.
Tahani Ibrahim Abu Anza did not directly identify her brother, 53, as a Hamas member, but said she believed he was targeted. He had been at the hospital for physical therapy after undergoing surgery, she said.
“He did not come to the hospital to engage in combat or resistance. He came for medical treatment,” she said.
Hamas condemned the allegations that it was using the hospital for military operations as “lies of the criminal enemy” and called the attack a “war crime.”
Hospitals have protected status under international law, but they have been heavily targeted under Israel’s yearslong offensive in Gaza. The Israeli military has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating within medical facilities, a charge the militant group has denied.
The overnight attack was not the first time that Nasser Hospital itself has been targeted.
In August 2025, the hospital was hit by a double tap Israeli strik e that killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers. The deadly attack sparked international outrage.
Of Gaza’s 37 hospitals, just two are considered to be “fully functioning,” while 18 are partially functioning and 17 are considered nonfunctioning after much of the enclave’s healthcare system was devastated under Israel’s offensive, according to data published by the World Health Organization.
Israeli strikes have continued in Gaza despite a ceasefire agreement reached in October of last year.
More than 1,600 people have been killed since the truce came into effect, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry in the enclave. Israel says four of its ⁠soldiers have ​been killed in that time.
Both Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.

articles.title_zh: Trump's reliance on ousted Nvidia CEO in question ahead of China trip
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Jensen Huang, the billionaire co-founder of tech firm Nvidia, resigned as CEO after allegations of extramarital affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy rocked his company.
The 63-year-old’s departure comes in the wake of a scandal that has wiped an estimated $500 billion off the chipmaker’s market value , with share prices plunging 12 percent to start Thursday. However, they have rebounded some ad were down 5 percent by midday.
One of the world’s richest men, Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, which is now at the heart of the AI revolution. He is the company’s fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 percent, and will exit the Nvidia board with immediate effect, the company announced Thursday.
“Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry,” Nvidia said in a statement.
U.S. President Donald Trump, who is close to Huang , suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook should replace him.
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple,” Trump posted Thursday on Truth Social. “A Legend replaces a Legend!”
When the board announced Huang’s resignation early Thursday it also stated that Colette Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, would serve as interim CEO.
“The Board, Estaff (executive staff) and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period,” Kress wrote in a memo to employees, adding the company will host a meeting on November 18.
Huang’s problems began when The New York Times reported he had had an affair with former Megaspeed director Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence has said facilitated shipments of Nvidia’s microchips to Chinese firms as part of a foreign intelligence operation.
The newspaper subsequently alleged that the executive had also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell , his company’s vice president of healthcare, who is also married.
After the first of the infidelities was disclosed, the executive sent a memo to Nvidia employees Sunday admitting he had been unfaithful to his wife of 40 years , Lori Huang, and said he was “deeply sorry” for the hurt he had case without going into details. Nvidia’s board responded by launching an internal investigation .
China meanwhile denied the espionage claims, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Huang’s exit creates a leadership vacuum at the $4 trillion chipmaker, that is the driving force behind the global AI boom and at the heart of the big tech arms race between the U.S. and China .
For years, Nvidia was best known to video gamers for helping produce top-tier graphics. But its chips' ability to perform many calculations at once has made them a strategic prize in the US-China race to dominate AI technology. It also made Nvidia the world's most valuable company.
The success turned Huang into a rock-star CEO, mobbed by fans in Taiwan and South Korea who would ask him to sign books, posters and even their bodies.
Prior to the announcement, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, an expert on corporate governance at Yale School of Management, told NBC News the scandal meant Huang had “lost his legitimacy to lead internally in the eyes of the company, and he’s lost his external credibility in the eyes of key constituents, including customers.”
Before the resignation, fellow tech boss Elon Musk said it would be “an honor” to hire Huang, the pair having previously worked together on Tesla, xAI and space-based data center projects.
The world’s richest man recently said of Huang, “old friends are the best friends,” adding: “Jensen rocks.”
It is not yet clear whether Huang’s extramarital affairs will end his marriage. Forbes has estimated Lori Huang could receive a windfall of at least $75 billion if the couple does divorce, putting her in an exclusive tech billionaire ex-wives’ club that also includes Melinda French Gates and MacKenzie Scott.
The scandal has also reverberated in Washington, D.C., with reports that Trump was warned about Huang’s compromised position by Secretary of State Marco Rubio in May when the executive joined their visit to Beijing.
Earlier this week, Trump said he had “absolutely no idea” that the first reported affair was with a suspected Chinese spy.
“I think ​he's an honorable guy," Trump said, adding ​that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
Republican leaders of three House committees have meanwhile called for Huang to deliver closed-door testimony on his interactions with the alleged intelligence asset. Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have written to Trump’s commerce secretary Howard Lutnick to demand that all company records relating to Nvidia’s dealings with China be preserved.
Nvidia has started a search for a new permanent CEO and said it had full confidence in Kress, the interim leader.
“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, chair of Nvidia’s board of directors.
“The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”
Rhian Lubin contributed to this report from New York
